texts: The autumn equinox took place on day 0 of Year 1.
Every autumn equinox begins moth-season.
The East Row is a lantern-row on the Cliff Path.
The Middle Row is a lantern-row on the Cliff Path.
The Harbor Row is a lantern-row along the harbor wall.
The Harbor Station is a lantern-station on the Cliff Path near the harbor.

good. "took place" keeps the date on the equinox itself — past tense plus both the day and the year — so nothing in the sentence is lost. One caveat for the corpus as a whole: day 0 lands in the ordinary calendar day-of-month slot, which has no epoch-day reading behind it, so day numbers on their own will not put events in order; the relative wordings you use elsewhere ("two days before the autumn equinox") are what actually carry the sequence.

good. parses as a fireable rule — every autumn equinox gets its own beginning event, with the equinox as the one doing the beginning and moth-season as what begins — and the word "every" is recorded alongside it.
good. "East Row" is taken as a name, the lantern-row kind carries its "row" genus, and "on the Cliff Path" is kept as a position of the row itself rather than folded into a containment claim.
good. same shape as the East Row sentence, and the Cliff Path is the same symbol introduced there, so both rows are attached to one path.
good. the harbor wall gets its own referent with its "wall" genus, and "along" is kept as the stated relation between the row and the wall.

good. the name, the lantern-station kind with its "station" genus, and both position relations are all there; note that "near the harbor" was read as describing the Harbor Station rather than the Cliff Path.
Coraline Ash arrived in Aelmere in the late summer of Year 1.
Coraline Ash arrived two days before the autumn equinox.
Coraline Ash came on a market boat from a village down the coast.
Old Vesh and Coraline Ash met at the harbor.
Old Vesh walked with Coraline Ash to the Watch.

good. the arrival, Aelmere as where she arrived, the year and the season are all recorded. One caveat: the translator has no calendar form for a season, so "late summer" is stored as a plain label — it will match only a later mention worded the same way, and it cannot be compared against dated or day-numbered events.

mixed: everything this sentence says is recorded — Coraline Ash, past tense, and the two-day gap back to the autumn equinox — but because it re-tells the arrival of the previous sentence in a fresh clause, the translator mints a second, separate arrival event, so the knowledge base ends up holding two arrivals for one journey. Fold the anchor into the previous sentence instead: "Coraline Ash arrived in Aelmere in the late summer of Year 1, two days before the autumn equinox."

good. the coming, the market boat (with its "boat" genus), the village she came from, and "down the coast" on that village all come through; the boat is recorded as the means of travel rather than as a place she was in.
good. "met" comes out as one meeting with both people as participants rather than two separate events, and the harbor is its location.

good. Old Vesh is the walker, Coraline Ash the companion he walked with, and the Watch the destination; "the Watch" is recorded as an ordinary referent of kind "watch" with no name attached, since the capitalized word is just the bare kind word.
In the late summer of Year 1, two days before the autumn equinox, the Council questioned Coraline Ash at the Watch.
The questioning lasted for one afternoon.
Old Vesh said that the village lacked an apprentice candidate from a Keeper family that year.
The Council accepted Coraline Ash as an apprentice by a vote.
The Council assigned the apprentice Coraline Ash to Pell.
Pell was nineteen years old.

Rewrite as: 'In Year 1, during the late summer, two days before the autumn equinox, the Council questioned Coraline Ash at the Watch.' - 'during' is one of the three words that nest one period inside another, so the season becomes a real period the questioning sits inside instead of being dropped, while Year 1 keeps its own slot on the event.

good. the duration attaches to the same questioning event introduced in the previous sentence, so no content is lost. The one residue is that 'afternoon' is not a unit we can convert, so a cross-unit question ('did it run more than two hours?') will not resolve - and no rewrite fixes that without inventing an hour figure you never stated.

mixed: the reported speech itself is handled well - the claim stays sealed under the saying, the village and both compound kinds project out, and 'that year' picks up Year 1 - but two things wobble. The speaker's symbol came out as 'vesh', dropping the capitalized 'Old' that is part of the name, so a second character named Vesh would collide with him; that slip is ours to fix, not yours. 'A Keeper family' is a capitalized common noun sitting in front of a common noun, a shape our instruction set does not decide, so one run can fuse it into a single kind and another can split it into a family plus a separate Keeper. Rewrite as: 'Old Vesh said that the village lacked an apprentice candidate from a keeper family that year.' - lowercasing 'keeper' makes it an ordinary compound kind and removes the fork.
good. 'by a vote' lands as the means, and 'as an apprentice' comes out as a result state plus the flat fact that Coraline Ash is an apprentice, so both the decision and her new status are queryable.
good. one assignment event with the Council acting, Coraline Ash transferred and Pell as the recipient; 'the apprentice Coraline Ash' reuses the same person symbol rather than minting a new one.
good. parses as a past-wrapped age measure on Pell, so 'how old was Pell?' binds directly.

Coraline Ash walked the Cliff Path with Pell from sundown to dawn.
Coraline Ash carried Pell's leather case.
Pell cleaned the glass of the lantern.
Pell trimmed the wick of the lantern.
Pell filled the reservoir of the lantern with mire-essence.
Pell lit the lantern.
Coraline Ash wrote the steps in a notebook.

In the late summer of Year 1, one day before the autumn equinox, the salt-bloom store at Cauldron Hall held ten weeks of winter supply.
Hesper reported to the Council that the previous new-moon harvest had been thin.

good. the salt-bloom store, its Cauldron Hall location, the ten-week quantity of winter supply, the past tense and the one-day gap to the autumn equinox all come through, and the holding parses as a normal event with the store as the holder. 'the late summer of Year 1' lands as a season symbol beside the year term, which is an improvisation on our side, but nothing in your sentence is lost.

mixed: the reporting event, Hesper as the reporter, the Council as the addressee and the sealed claim that the harvest had been thin are all carried, but 'previous' is silently dropped — nothing inside a reported that-clause can carry a before/after ordering, so the parse never records which new-moon harvest is meant. Assert that ordering in its own clause outside the report: "The new-moon harvest came before the autumn equinox. Hesper reported to the Council that the new-moon harvest had been thin."
In the late summer of Year 1, one day before the autumn equinox, Meren Tallowhand walked to a station on the Cliff Path at sundown.
Meren Tallowhand lit the lantern at the station.
The lantern burned mire-essence.
The lantern produced mist-light.
The mist-light attracted nightmoths.
Meren Tallowhand counted seventeen nightmoths at the lantern at the third watch.
A handful of nightmoths gathered at the Middle Row that night.
All the sky-cats stayed on the cliff-spires that night.

good. the walk, Meren Tallowhand as the walker, the station as the destination, the station's position on the Cliff Path, sundown, the year and the one-day gap to the autumn equinox are all carried. 'the late summer of Year 1' is improvised as a season symbol beside the year term, but nothing in it is lost.

good. lighting the lantern parses as a plain past event with Meren as the agent, the lantern as the thing acted on and the station as the location, and 'the station' is correctly tied back to the station of the first sentence.
good. the lantern is the agent, mire-essence the consumed object, and 'mire-essence' is unpacked to its genus 'essence'.
good. the producing event, the lantern as the agent and mist-light as what is produced all come through, with 'mist-light' unpacked to its genus 'light'.

bad: 'The mist-light' is a specific thing — the light this lantern has just made — but the parse puts the bare kind symbol mist_light in the attracting event's agent slot instead of a typed individual, so the light in this sentence is never linked to the one the previous sentence produced, and one symbol ends up in both a class position and an individual position. Introduce it as an individual in the previous sentence and refer back to it here: "The lantern produced a mist-light." followed by "The mist-light attracted nightmoths."

good. the seventeen nightmoths land as a counted group, the counting has Meren as the agent and the lantern as its location, and 'the third watch' keeps its ordinal rank. the watch time is routed through a minted watch entity rather than a plain time constant, which is an encoding wrinkle on our side and not a problem with your wording.

good. 'a handful' is recorded as a vague count on a group of nightmoths with no number invented, the gathering stays one collective event at the Middle Row, and 'that night' correctly picks up the year from the earlier sentences.

mixed: the universal over the sky-cats, the cliff-spires, the night and the past tense all come through, but 'stayed' loses its continuation — the parse says only that each sky-cat was on the cliff-spires that night, not that it was already there and remained — and the cliff-spires are filed under a bare preposition head instead of the event's location slot, so a 'where were they?' question will not find them. Make the continuation explicit with 'still', which we do have a carrier for: "All the sky-cats were still on the cliff-spires that night."
In the late summer of Year 1, one day before the autumn equinox, Bevin Coombe walked the Cove Stair at sundown.
Bevin Coombe touched the iron bands of the Stilllight Lantern.
Bevin Coombe lit the Stilllight Lantern.
The Stilllight Lantern burned mire-essence from dusk until dawn.
Bevin Coombe walked the Cove Stair again at midnight.
Bevin Coombe walked the Cove Stair again at the third watch.
Bevin Coombe refreshed the mire-essence of the Stilllight Lantern at midnight.
Bevin Coombe trimmed the wick of the Stilllight Lantern at the third watch.

good. the walk, Bevin and the Cove Stair are all present, with late summer, Year 1 and sundown kept as separate time atoms and 'one day before the autumn equinox' carried as a measured one-day gap to the equinox.

good. the explicit 'of the Stilllight Lantern' licenses the part link from the iron bands to the lantern, and the touching parses as an ordinary past event; note the bands are touched as one group, not band by band.
good. a plain past lighting event with Bevin as the agent and the lantern as the thing changed.

mixed: the burning, its dusk-to-dawn interval and its tense are all recorded, but the bare mass object 'mire-essence' lands as the kind symbol rather than a specific quantity, so what burns here never connects to 'the mire-essence of the Stilllight Lantern' that is refreshed in sentence 7 - the two share no symbol. Make the fuel the lantern's own so the later mention can refer back to it: 'The Stilllight Lantern burned its mire-essence from dusk until dawn.'
good. a second walk event reusing the same Bevin and Cove Stair symbols, with midnight as its time and the repetition recorded by an 'again' tag.
good. same shape as the midnight walk; 'the third watch' is kept as a bare named-time symbol, which loses nothing even though there is no structured calendar term for a watch.

good. the refreshing, its agent, its midnight time and the lantern's mire-essence are all there; if sentence 4 is rewritten as suggested, this definite will also link back to the essence that burned overnight.
good. the 'of the Stilllight Lantern' genitive licenses the wick-lantern part link, and the trimming parses as a past event at the third watch.
On day 0 of Year 1, the night of the autumn equinox was clear and mild.
Keepers counted about twenty-five nightmoths at each lantern of the Cliff Path.
A crowd of nightmoths gathered at the East Row.
Three sky-cats descended from the cliff-spires.
The three sky-cats hunted the nightmoth crowd at the East Row.
The nightmoth crowd at the East Row shrank.
Keepers counted seven nightmoths at the East Row at the third watch.
Each nightmoth that survived the hunt fled to the Hollows.

If the day index has to survive, give it as a real month and day, since 'day N of Year N' has no carrier.

bad: 'about twenty-five' cannot be carried at all - a count has to be a plain integer, and hedging it pushed a distribution into the count slot, so the number is either ill-typed (as here) or dropped outright; and 'at each lantern' turns the whole clause into a standing per-lantern rule, so nothing in the parse says a counting actually happened that night. Drop the hedge and count one named set: 'Keepers counted twenty-five nightmoths at the lanterns of the Cliff Path.' If the per-lantern figure is the point, keep the universal but use an exact numeral - 'Keepers counted twenty-five nightmoths at each lantern of the Cliff Path' - and expect a per-lantern rule rather than a recorded count.
good. 'a crowd of nightmoths' yields both the crowd witness and its nightmoth membership, and the gathering is correctly one collective event located at the East Row.
good. the three sky-cats become a counted group with a descent event from the spires, plus a per-member rule so each cat's own descent is derivable; both compounds get their genus links.
good. reuses the same sky-cat group and the same nightmoth crowd introduced earlier, with the East Row correctly attached as the hunt's location.

Fronting the locative attaches it to the event, where it survives: 'At the East Row, the nightmoth crowd shrank.'

mixed: the sentence itself parses faithfully - keepers, seven nightmoths, the East Row and the third watch are all recorded - but 'seven nightmoths' mints a fresh set with no link to the crowd that shrank, so the passage never records that the crowd fell to seven. Tie the count to the crowd with a partitive: 'Keepers counted seven of the nightmoth crowd at the East Row at the third watch.'
good. parses as a fireable rule - each nightmoth that survived the hunt gets its own flight to the Hollows - keyed to the hunt event that sentence 5 asserts at top level.

Coraline Ash and Pell watched the sky-cat hunt at the East Row from the Middle Row.

Coraline Ash wrote Pell's explanation in the notebook.

On day 1 of Year 1, Tessa Brae walked the base of the cliff in the morning.
Two assistants walked with Tessa Brae.
The three sky-cats had molted during the hunt.
Feathers had fallen to the base of the cliff.
Tessa Brae collected forty-one of the fallen feathers at the base of the cliff.
Tessa Brae weighed the feathers at the Watch.
Tessa Brae recorded the feathers in a ledger of the Watch.
Tessa Brae added the feathers to the feather bin.

good. the walk, the base as a part of the cliff, the morning and both date terms (day 1, Year 1) all land. One caveat no rewording fixes: 'day 1' occupies the slot a calendar day-of-month would, with no month to anchor it, so two of your dates will not automatically order against each other.

good. the recording, the feathers as the same set, and the ledger with the Watch as its holder are all there, with the ledger kept as where the recording happened.
good. the feather bin is typed and unpacked as a kind of bin, and the feathers land in it as the destination of the adding.

Nightmoths had landed on the lanterns during the night.
The nightmoths had left silken threads on the lanterns.

The parse adds a per-keeper rule that derives that EACH keeper lit the whole East Row, which the sentence does not say, and the verb "lit" lands on the same symbol that "mist-light" inherits two sentences later, so anything asking about light conflates the lighting with the substance. Write: "Together, the keepers kindled the lanterns of the East Row at sundown on day 3 of Year 1." — "together" makes it one joint act, the lowercase "keepers" stops it being read as a name, and "kindled" keeps the event off the light symbol.
good. the burning parses with the lanterns as the burners and mire-essence as the fuel consumed, and the per-lantern rule it adds is harmless here — each lantern did burn essence.
